meta.title: Who really said "Good judgment comes from experience, and a lot of that comes from bad judgment"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Will Rogers. The saying was in print anonymously by 1932; the Rogers credit traces to a forwarded email reprinted in a newspaper in 2000.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Good judgment comes from experience, and a lot of that comes from bad judgment'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Will Rogers. Anonymous in print by 1932, credited to "Uncle Zeke" in 1945, and pinned on Rogers only by a chain email decades after his death.

answer.label: Not Will Rogers — an anonymous saying
answer.authorDates: Unattributed American saying · in print by February 1932
answer.sourceLine: No Will Rogers column, daily telegram, film line or book has ever been produced that contains this sentence, and it appears nowhere in the sourced or misattributed lists on his Wikiquote page. The saying was already circulating anonymously while Rogers was alive — the earliest match Quote Investigator located is a February 1932 Indiana newspaper item that credits no one, and the only Rogers-credited citation the same article documents is a March 2000 column reprinting a forwarded email — whose own columnist added that the line was “probably never said by Rogers.”

source.heading: The earliest documented appearance

docMeta.dd: No one — quoted as a floating remark at a Rotary Club meeting

source.excerpt: Good Judgment depends mostly on experience and experience usually comes from poor judgment.
trail: 1932 — anonymous from the start. The earliest match located by Quote Investigator ran in The Muncie Evening Press on 17 February 1932, where a speaker named Fred Rose quoted it at a Rotary Club meeting in a way that signalled the saying was already common property.

1943–1945 — still ownerless. A 1943 Baltimore Sun item repeats it in dialect with no named author; in April 1945 Reader's Digest ran the anecdote in which Lt. Gen. Simon Bolivar Buckner Jr. credits “Uncle Zeke” of his Kentucky home town. Newspapers reprinted the Zeke story that December.

1986–2001 — the names arrive. Robert Byrne's collection assigned it to Barry LePatner; Rita Mae Brown used it in 2001 as an old saying. Neither is an origin, and Quote Investigator's conclusion is that the saying was anonymous in its earliest instances.

Rogers's own record is silent. The line appears nowhere in the sourced, attributed or misattributed sections of Wikiquote's Will Rogers page, and the Will Rogers Memorial Museum — which cautions that some quotes credited to him are falsely credited — does not list it either.
source.excerptNote: This is the wording of the earliest known appearance, not the modern popular phrasing. The familiar “and a lot of that comes from bad judgment” version is a later smoothing, documented in the Rogers-credited email column of 2000.

source.rightsNote: No copyright status can honestly be asserted, because no author and no originating work are known. The earliest documented printing is a 1932 newspaper item that names no author, and the modern popular wording is a later, unsourced smoothing — so this is an orphan saying rather than an excerpt from an identifiable work. Quotle.info does not claim public-domain status for text it cannot tie to a specific pre-1931 source.

author.name: Will Rogers
author.heading: The man the quote gets pinned on
author.metaLine: 1879–1935 · American humorist, newspaper columnist and film star
author.bio: William Penn Adair Rogers, a citizen of the Cherokee Nation born near Oologah in Indian Territory, went from rope-trick vaudevillian to the Ziegfeld Follies, then to 71 films and more than 4,000 syndicated newspaper columns between 1922 and his death. He died in a plane crash near Utqiaġvik, Alaska, on 15 August 1935, alongside aviator Wiley Post. This particular saying is not his — it is included here because his name is the one most often stamped on it, a hazard of being America's most quotable plain-spoken wit.

copyAttribution: "Good judgment comes from experience, and a lot of that comes from bad judgment." — not Will Rogers. The saying is anonymous: its earliest documented appearance is an unattributed remark in The Muncie Evening Press, 17 February 1932, worded "Good Judgment depends mostly on experience and experience usually comes from poor judgment." misattribution.heading: Who has been credited — and why none of it holds
misattribution.intro: This is a genuinely ownerless aphorism, and ownerless aphorisms collect names. At least four have been attached to it, none supported by a primary source.

items.why: No pre-2000 citation credits him. Quote Investigator documents exactly one Rogers-credited instance — a March 2000 column in Florida Today reprinting a forwarded email of “Will Rogers' wisdom” — and the columnist himself flagged that the line was “probably never said by Rogers.” The saying is absent from his Wikiquote page entirely, and from the Will Rogers Memorial Museum's quote page.

Robert Byrne's 1986 quotation collection printed the saying under LePatner's name, and reference sites followed — The Quotations Page still lists it that way, with no source. The saying predates that credit by more than fifty years.
Brown used the expression in her 2001 novel Alma Mater and helped popularise it, but Quote Investigator notes she presented it as an old saying rather than her own coinage.

items.scope: The oldest named source — and still not an author
items.why: An April 1945 Reader's Digest anecdote has Lieutenant General Simon Bolivar Buckner Jr. attribute the line to a wise old man from his Kentucky home town. Uncle Zeke is a figure in a told story, not a documented speaker — and the saying was already in print thirteen years earlier.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer is that nobody knows who said it first. The earliest surviving appearance, per Quote Investigator, is an unattributed remark quoted at a Rotary Club meeting and printed in The Muncie Evening Press on 17 February 1932.

context.heading: Why this one sticks to Will Rogers
lead: The line has a shape Rogers made famous — homespun, self-deprecating, a punchline that arrives by doubling back on itself. That is exactly what makes it dangerous: an unowned aphorism drifts toward whichever dead humorist it sounds most like, and for plain-spoken American wit that is almost always Rogers. Mark Twain absorbs the cynical ones; Rogers absorbs the folksy ones.

The paper trail runs the other way. In its earliest surviving appearances the saying belongs to nobody at all — a Rotarian quotes it in 1932 as a piece of floating wisdom, a wartime newspaper repeats it in 1943 with no named author, and a 1945 Reader's Digest anecdote hands it to a Kentucky old-timer called “Uncle Zeke,” who is himself a story character rather than a documented person. Rogers's name does not enter the record until the chain-email era.
detailsBody: 1943, The Baltimore Sun. The saying resurfaces rendered in folksy dialect and is still credited to no named author — only to an unnamed source of homely wisdom, per Quote Investigator's citation list.

1945, Reader's Digest. An anecdote contributed by Brigadier General John W. Lang has Lieutenant General Simon Bolivar Buckner Jr. settle an argument by quoting “Uncle Zeke” of his Kentucky home town. The tale spread through newspapers that December, and it is the version most modern paraphrases descend from.

1986 onward. Robert Byrne's quotation collection printed the saying under the name of Barry LePatner, and reference sites picked that credit up. Rogers, LePatner, Rita Mae Brown and “Anonymous” have all carried it since — a signature pattern of a quote with no real owner.
context.pull: An unowned aphorism drifts toward whichever dead humorist it sounds most like.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's article gives the earliest match as The Muncie Evening Press, 17 February 1932, page 4, where Fred Rose quoted it anonymously at a Rotary Club meeting; documents 1943 Baltimore Sun, April 1945 Reader's Digest (Uncle Zeke via Simon Bolivar Buckner Jr., contributed by Brig. Gen. John W. Lang), 1986 Robert Byrne/Barry LePatner, 2000 Florida Today (Will Rogers via forwarded email, columnist noted 'The first one was probably never said by Rogers'), and 2001 Rita Mae Brown; and concludes 'The linkage to Will Rogers was unsupported.' No pre-2000 citation in the article credits Rogers.

Wikiquote's Will Rogers page does not contain 'Good judgment comes from experience' or any 'bad judgment' variant in any section, including its Misattributed section; the only 'judgment' hit is an unrelated Daily telegram about Judgment Day.

The Will Rogers Memorial Museum's official quotes page does not contain 'good judgment' or 'bad judgment', and states that some quotes attributed to Will Rogers are falsely credited, offering curator verification.

Will Rogers lived 4 November 1879 to 15 August 1935, was born near Oologah in Indian Territory, was a Cherokee Nation citizen, performed in vaudeville and the Ziegfeld Follies, starred in 71 films, wrote over 4,000 syndicated columns from 1922, and died in a plane crash near Utqiagvik, Alaska with Wiley Post.
Simon Bolivar Buckner Jr. (18 July 1886 - 18 June 1945) was a Kentucky native born in Munfordville and a lieutenant general in the US Army, killed at Okinawa.
The Quotations Page lists 'Good judgment comes from experience, and experience comes from bad judgment.' credited to Barry LePatner, with no original source cited.
